The dog involved is a Spanish Mastiff, named "Larry". (Photo provided by Hong Kong Animal News)

The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) said in the evening that it would prosecute the dog owner. The department stated that, under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, it would charge a 52-year-old man for failing to properly control his large dog; the department also said it would add further charges under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance. The dog involved, "Larry", has caused two deaths and one injury. The AFCD said the dog owner was suspected of failing, on at least two occasions in July and August this year, to properly leash the dog in public as required by law, during which the dog attacked three dogs — one was injured on 10 July, and two died on 17 August. The department said the case would be brought to Tuen Mun Magistrates' Court on Thursday (20th) for first mention. With strong public concern over "Larry"'s fate, the AFCD said the man had signed a consent form transferring custody of the dog to the department. The department said it would assess the dog's temperament to determine an appropriate course of action.

AFCD Assistant Director Yip Yin said today (19th) on RTHK programme "Millennium Era" that they would ascertain the wishes of the owner of the large dog involved. If the owner decided to hand the dog over to the government, the department would consider all options and, if necessary, would consider euthanasia. He said if the owner intended to take the dog back, the dog could be classified as a "known dangerous dog", and the court could order that the dog must wear a muzzle when out in public in future.

The large dog involved, "Larry". (Photo provided by Hong Kong Animal News)

Yip Yin said the large dog involved was a mixed breed weighing over 20 kg, and was under observation at the AFCD's Animal Management Centre. He said the incident happened on Monday and footage had circulated online, with members of the public believing there was solid evidence. He noted that once judicial proceedings commenced, the matter had to be handled rigorously, with various procedures to follow: "Regardless, our colleagues will follow up as quickly as possible."

(Photo provided by Hong Kong Animal News)

Kent, who set up the animal protection organisation Mao Mau Rescue, had contacted the owner of the large dog. To his knowledge, the dog is a Spanish Mastiff, five years old this year, normally kept inside the home, and had previously escaped by digging through the garden. He told Animal News that when the owner gave his statement yesterday, he was asked on the spot to sign an abandonment form, which he did; the owner later expressed regret, and heard some AFCD staff say the dog might be "dealt with".

Kent told Stand News today that the large dog is a five-year-old Spanish Mastiff named "Larry". The first owner once purchased two dogs of the same breed, including "Larry"; "Larry" was subsequently abandoned, went through second and third abandonments, and was ultimately taken in by the current owner.

Kent revealed that yesterday the owner went to the police station to sign documents, and today proactively called Mao Mau for help: "He thought 'dealing with' meant taking care of it for him; when he saw media reports this morning saying it meant euthanasia, he wanted even less to do that."

He added that "Larry" and the current owner live in a village hutment within one kilometre of YOHO; last month the dog escaped once — the previous incident that the public saw where it bit a Corgi. Kent helped handle the situation on site at the time. This time the dog again escaped after the owner went to work. However, based on his observation of "Larry" on both occasions, he judged the dog was not necessarily acting aggressively but rather "playing", because a dog attacking or hunting would shake and tear at its prey after biting it. "But even when people tried to separate them, it showed no attacking behaviour; even when AFCD went to catch it, it didn't." He stressed, however, that "Larry"'s situation was one of no training or restraint, noting that there are dogs in the New Territories that "chase cats and bite" as well, and he believed that with proper training a better outcome could be achieved.

Kent said the owner currently hopes to first stop the AFCD from euthanising the dog. He also said that if the AFCD agreed not to euthanise the dog, Mao Mau was willing to take it in and arrange a dog trainer to follow up: "People deserve a chance, and dogs deserve one too... killing the dog won't make things right."

At the pet park at Yuen Long YOHO Mall, a dog-bites-dog incident on Monday (17th) left bereaved owners kneeling helplessly on the ground — heartbreaking to witness. The large dog involved killed a Poodle and a Bichon Frise within a single day; police arrived and took the large dog away and handed it to the AFCD. The dog had previously been detained by the department on 10 July this year in connection with another dog-biting incident, and was subsequently reclaimed by its keeper. The AFCD said that under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, large dogs weighing 20 kg or above must be securely leashed with a lead no longer than two metres in public places. Violation may result in a fine of HK$25,000 and three months' imprisonment. Under Section 23 of the Rabies Ordinance, dogs must be leashed or otherwise properly controlled when in public places, or elsewhere where it may reasonably be expected that the dog would stray into a public place. Violation may result in a fine of HK$10,000.
